Thanks, this was really clean work. Merged and released in v0.2.0.

I added one commit on top before merging (2f68061): on Windows, `op` and `powershell` are now resolved through PATH with `Bun.which` instead of by bare name. Windows checks the current directory before PATH, so a planted `op.exe` or `powershell.exe` in an untrusted repo could otherwise have received the token or a secret. CI also runs on `windows-latest` now, including the real DPAPI store test, and both platforms passed.

issues.title: Security review: executable lookup, Bun preload scripts, and URL metadata can expose credentials
issues.body:
A security review found three credential exposure paths at commit `e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16`.

The checks used Windows and Bun 1.3.14. All credentials were fictional. No real 1Password account was accessed.

This issue gives the findings, source references, and test results. It omits executable payloads because SECURITY.md requests private vulnerability reports.

## 1. Windows executable lookup includes the current directory

Source: [src/op.ts:49–52](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/op.ts#L49-L52).

The comment states that executable lookup uses PATH only. However, `Bun.which("op")` returned `.\\op.exe` when the current directory contained that executable.

A controlled check ran the real `inventory` command from a directory with a fake `op.exe`. The fake executable received the fictional `OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN` and the arguments `item list --format json`. The command returned an empty inventory.

Expected behavior: a repository-local executable must not replace the trusted 1Password CLI.

Impact: a repository can supply an executable that receives the service-account token. The same lookup function also selects PowerShell for credential and clipboard operations.

Suggested correction: resolve executables through trusted absolute paths. Exclude the current directory and relative PATH entries.

## 2. Internal Bun helpers load repository preload scripts

Sources: [src/env.ts:76–90](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/env.ts#L76-L90), [src/op.ts:150–163](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/op.ts#L150-L163), and [src/without-token.ts:1–7](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/without-token.ts#L1-L7).

`readMany` starts `bun -e` with the caller's current directory. Bun loads scripts from the local `bunfig.toml` before it runs that helper.

A controlled check used the actual `readMany` function and a fake `op` that supplied a fictional resolved secret. A local preload script accessed the resolved secret and the fictional service-account token. The resolver still returned the expected value.

This check emulated credential injection. It did not use the real 1Password CLI.

The Windows token-removal helper also starts Bun before it deletes the token. Its protection therefore occurs after runtime preload scripts can run.

Expected behavior: internal credential helpers must not execute repository-controlled startup code.

Suggested correction: use a controlled directory and trusted runtime configuration for internal helpers. Remove unnecessary authentication credentials before helper startup.

Reference: [Bun preload documentation](https://bun.sh/docs/runtime/bunfig#preload).

## 3. Inventory and audit preserve secrets in URL paths

Sources: [src/discover.ts:82–89](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/discover.ts#L82-L89) and [inventory output](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/discover.ts#L203-L209).

`safeUrl` removes query strings and fragments but preserves paths. It also returns raw input before the query or fragment when URL parsing fails.

A source-level check confirmed that a reset URL with a fictional token in its path remained unchanged. Invalid relative URLs with embedded credentials also remained unchanged.

Expected behavior: metadata output must not expose credentials from saved URLs.

Suggested correction: output only valid HTTP(S) origins. Omit paths and reject invalid or unsupported URLs. For audit results, detect transient paths internally and return a fixed reason instead of the URL path.

## Validation and limits

- The existing suite passed 67 tests. One test was skipped.
- The Windows executable selection flaw was reproduced through the real CLI.
- The preload check used the actual resolver with emulated credential injection.
- The URL check executed the source-extracted filter with fictional values.
- macOS behavior and published npm artifacts were not verified.

These findings concern unintended credential consumers and metadata output. They are separate from the documented ability of a selected child process to disclose its injected credentials.

issues.title: RFC: separate secret injection from destination-bound secret use
issues.body:
Thanks for putting this together — the existing invariants are unusually strong for such a new tool: refs-only discovery, fixed failure messages around plaintext, no automatic write retries, read-back verification, and explicit service-account narrowing.

I think there is one security boundary worth naming early because it affects the core promise.

## Problem

Today `2password run` keeps a value out of the model/context while resolving it, but then places it in an agent-chosen child process environment and streams that child's stdout/stderr back normally.

That is useful **secret injection**, but it is not yet enforceable **secret use without reveal**: a compromised/prompt-injected agent can choose a child that prints the variable or sends it to an arbitrary destination.

I would keep `run` — it is useful — but distinguish it from a stronger capability.

## Proposed model

Keep 1Password as **custody** and make 2password the narrow **authority + private execution** layer:

```
1Password custody
    ↓ op:// handle
2password authority
    ↓ short-lived capability
private executor
    ↓
destination
    ↓
sanitized receipt
```

The key split is:

- `secret.use`: the caller may cause an allowed operation with a secret but never receive the value.
- `secret.reveal`: the caller may receive plaintext. `read` / `env resolve` are explicitly in this class.
- `run` remains an injection primitive and should document that the child is inside the trust boundary.

## Smallest strong primitive

A structured destination-bound request path, e.g. `2password request` / `2password broker http`:

- secret identified only by `op://...`
- exact HTTPS destination host
- no redirects, userinfo, or caller-controlled host override
- resolve/check public IPs before connect
- secret inserted internally into an approved header/field
- bounded response size
- redact exact injected values if the destination echoes them
- return a typed receipt, never the credential

This is much easier to reason about than trying to make arbitrary `run` commands non-revealing.

## Authority / leases

For unattended agents, machine identity should authenticate the caller but initially grant zero resources.

A human approval can mint a short-lived lease bound to:

`principal + resource + field + capability + destination + resource version/fingerprint + expiry + atomic use budget`

That gives us "approve once for this exact use" without turning a service-account token into blanket vault authority. Rotation invalidates stale leases automatically via the resource fingerprint/version.

## PII / egress

Two layers, deliberately separate:

1. **Destination binding/private execution is the privacy boundary.**
2. PII/secret redaction on tool/provider egress is a last guardrail for accidental echo, not an authorization mechanism.

Receipts should contain only bounded metadata: action, handle/item identity, destination, outcome, timing, and lease/use counters.

## Service-account note

The existing dedicated-vault service account is a good narrowing mechanism. Longer-term I would avoid treating "token is in Keychain" as authority by itself: an arbitrary local agent running as the same user should not inherit the ability to turn that token into unrestricted plaintext reads. Ideally the broker is the only component that can exercise it.

## Incremental path

1. Document the current `run` / `env run` trust boundary.
2. Add the structured destination-bound request primitive with exact-secret echo redaction and tests.
3. Add policy + non-secret receipts.
4. Add caller identity and short-lived leases for unattended use.
5. Only then consider a resident broker/daemon if prompt reduction justifies it.

## Non-goals

- replacing 1Password as custody
- weakening the existing "writes run once" invariant
- generic authenticated HTTP as a giant new surface
- using PII detection as the primary security boundary
- trying to make arbitrary child-process execution provably model-blind

## Provenance / related work

This builds directly on the security shape already established here by @kitlangton.

Related experiments/design work that may save us from re-learning the same edges:

- NousResearch/hermes-agent#107700 — destination-bound credential handles / `use != reveal`
- NousResearch/hermes-agent#107698 — why process-wide env hydration is the wrong long-term boundary
- NousResearch/hermes-agent#102922 — local PII egress redaction, explicitly treated as a guardrail rather than the privacy boundary
- pass-cli/passd experiments: zero-authority machine identities, exact HITL leases, destination binding, and sanitized receipts

Happy to implement the smallest slice rather than trying to land the whole architecture at once.

discussion.body:
I pushed a deliberately narrow downstream prototype here: https://github.com/kvnloo/2password/pull/2

A couple of things changed while threat-modeling it:

- destination validation + all DNS resolution happens before the credential is read
- the TLS connection is pinned to one validated public address, with no redirect following
- the first version is now **receipt-only**: the HTTP response body never crosses back to the agent. Exact-secret echoes are counted, but even unrelated response PII/new tokens stay private.
- the receipt fingerprints the exact full URL while displaying only origin + path, so query values don't need to be surfaced for auditability

I kept it GET-only and limited to `Authorization` / `X-API-Key` on purpose. No arbitrary body/method surface, leases, daemon, or policy engine yet.

The design question I'd value your take on before promoting code upstream: does this stronger capability belong directly beside `run` as something like `request`, or would you rather keep the CLI's current model simple and put authority/private execution under a separate namespace/component?

Also not asking for a merge yet: the fork's Actions haven't started for the draft, and I want the normal check suite green before turning it into an upstream PR.

Progress update: #2 is merged, and the next isolated slice is now #6.

#6 is intentionally executor-only (no leases/policy/daemon) and is green on the full current `0.2.0` matrix:
- macOS: format/lint/typecheck/tests/package hygiene
- Windows: same + the real DPAPI `test:keychain`

It keeps the response body private entirely, validates all DNS answers before reading the credential, pins one validated public address, and returns receipt metadata only.

I'm keeping the authority/lease experiment downstream until this private-execution seam has had a chance to land/review, rather than making #6 carry two architectural decisions at once.
